newsitem.title: GERMANY: German prostitutes seek end to unfair treatment.
newsitem.headline: German prostitutes seek end to unfair treatment.

text.p: Germany's 400,000 prostitutes, fed up with taxation without representation, launched a campaign on Friday aimed at giving their profession legal status and official recognition.

Although prostitution is legal in Germany, those who admit they earn their living in the trade are denied health care, unemployment and retirement benefits. The government, nevertheless, collects taxes from them.

"Prostitutes are being legally exploited by the government," said Irmingard Schewe-Gerigk, a member of the Greens party that is to introduce legislation into parliament next week seeking to give prostitutes full legal rights.

"The hypocrisy has to end," she said at a news conference. "On the one hand, the government says prostitution is immoral and denies them full rights, but on the other hand it collects tax money. This is discrimination against women."

The leader of one prostitute group, Christine Droessler, said legal recognition would raise the public standing of the profession, making it safer and ultimately leading to lower prices for the end user.

"There have been a number of court decisions pointing to the discrepancy -- collecting taxes from professionals the state doesn't recognise," she said. "This shows that the state is the biggest pimp there is."

Droessler, leader of the Frankfurt group "Whores Defend Themselves Together", said it was only reasonable for prostitutes to have the right to sign binding contracts, sue clients for unpaid bills, and write off business-related costs such as brothel rent, furniture, work clothing or contraception.
"Once prostitution is recognised as a profession, much of the criminal element would disappear and the rents would fall because the profiteers would be out of business," she said.

The Greens said more than one million men use the services of the country's 400,000 prostitutes each day. They collect an estimated 12.5 billion marks ($9 billion) each year, although the prostitutes' profit is a small fraction of that total, Droessler said.
Although many prostitutes try to avoid paying taxes, Droessler said tax collectors regularly raid their flats and confiscate their records.
"Sometimes the women are hit with tax bills of up to 100,000 to 200,000 marks that are based on wild imaginations," she said.
Tax authorities assume prostitutes have four to six clients per day and simply assess a tax bill without allowing them to deduct their expenses, she said.
The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said on Friday they planned to introduce draft legislation of their own next week that would eliminate the legal discrimination of prostitutes.

Schewe-Gerigk said she was confident the liberal Free Democrats (FDP) would support the bid to give prostitutes full legal rights, but admitted it was unlikely Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) would back the bill.
